name: German East Africa
info: The German colony of the African Great Lakes region, taking in present-day mainland Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, remembered for the violence of its conquest, the Maji Maji Rebellion and Lettow-Vorbeck's wartime campaign.

facts.founder: Carl Peters and his Society for German Colonization, under an imperial charter signed by Chancellor Otto von Bismarck in 1885
facts.predecessor: The mainland claims of the Sultan of Zanzibar; the chiefdoms with which Peters signed treaties; the protectorate of the German East Africa Company
facts.successor: Tanganyika (British), the districts of Ruanda and Urundi (Belgian) and the Kionga Triangle (Portuguese Mozambique), as League of Nations mandates from 10 January 1920

t: German rule began with Carl Peters' treaties with mainland chieftains and an imperial charter of 1885, and was imposed on the coast when Bismarck's warships forced the Sultan of Zanzibar to accept the German claims.
The conquest was marked by widespread atrocities, and the Maji Maji Rebellion of 1905 was crushed by measures to create a famine that may have cost as many as 300,000 lives.
After Germany's defeat in the First World War the colony was divided: Tanganyika went to Britain, Ruanda and Urundi to Belgium and the Kionga Triangle to Portugal.
dyk: Germany never formally abolished slavery in German East Africa: in 1914 officials considered a ban but did not make one, since they did not think it financially possible to compensate the owners.

sections.foundation:
The colony began with the treaties that Carl Peters, an adventurer and the founder of the Society for German Colonization, signed with several chieftains on the mainland opposite Zanzibar. On 3 March 1885 the German government announced an imperial charter, signed by Chancellor Otto von Bismarck on 27 February, which granted Peters' company a protectorate in the African Great Lakes region. Peters' specialists then explored south to the Rufiji River and north to Witu, near Lamu. The Sultan of Zanzibar protested that he ruled the mainland as well as the islands; Bismarck sent five warships, which arrived on 7 August 1885 and trained their guns on the Sultan's palace, and the Sultan was forced to accept the German claims outside a coastal strip of 16 kilometres.

In November 1886 Germany and Britain agreed to respect the Sultan's sovereignty over his islands and that strip, and divided the mainland between themselves into spheres of interest; the Sultan had no option but to agree. German rule was established quickly over Bagamoyo, Dar es Salaam and Kilwa. The colony proper was organised when the German military was called in to put down a revolt against the German East Africa Company, the Abushiri Revolt of 1888, crushed with British help the following year. The Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty of 1890 settled the border with the British East Africa Protectorate.
sections.socioeconomy:
In the early years hunting and gathering remained the basis of the export economy, and ivory and wild rubber were the main exports. European-owned plantations multiplied but many proved unprofitable in unstable world markets; only sisal, grown on over 40,000 hectares, gave the large estates a reliable income. Two million coffee trees were planted, rubber covered 81,000 hectares and there were large cotton plantations. About 70,000 Africans worked on the plantations; local officials often colluded with landowners in forcing them to work, although Berlin had banned forced labour, and labour migration devastated 'labour reservoirs' such as Unyamwezi and Usukuma. Gold was found near Lake Victoria in 1894, and the Sekenke Gold Mine opened in 1909.

The Germans never formally abolished slavery. New enslavement and the commercial slave trade were banned in 1901 and all children born after 1905 were born free, but private sales went on: thousands of slaves, mostly women, were sold in 1911–1914, while thousands of others bought their freedom or left their enslavers. On the eve of the First World War the colony, the most populous of the German Empire, had more than 7.5 million inhabitants, about 30% of them Muslim, against around 10,000 Europeans, of whom 3,579 were Germans.
sections.military:
German expansion was carried out by military groups such as the Wissmann Truppe, African soldiers under German commanders armed with modern weapons, who committed widespread atrocities. Carl Peters earned the name 'Mkono-wa-damu', 'Man with the blood-stained hands', for the villages slaughtered in his conquests; rape, floggings and torture with iron rods were common, and other European powers called the German colonies the 'flogging colonies'. The Hehe under Chief Mkwawa resisted from 1891 to 1894 and were defeated because rival peoples supported the Germans; after years of guerrilla war Mkwawa, cornered, killed himself in 1898. The Maji Maji Rebellion of 1905 was put down by Governor Gustav Adolf von Götzen, who ordered measures to create a famine; it may have cost as many as 300,000 lives.

On 1 January 1914 the Schutztruppe garrisons numbered 110 German officers, 126 non-commissioned officers and 2,472 Askari. In the First World War General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck led 3,500 Europeans and 12,000 Askari and porters against a British army of 40,000, at times under Jan Smuts. At the Battle of Tanga in November 1914 his forces defeated a British force more than eight times larger, and his guerrilla war tied down British resources and inflicted more than 10,000 casualties. The light cruiser SMS Königsberg was scuttled in the Rufiji delta in July 1915, and her guns joined the land forces.
sections.governance:
Carl Peters was the company's administrator from 27 May 1885 to 8 February 1888. After the Abushiri Revolt the Reich took over: Hermann Wissmann served as Reichskommissar from 1888 to 1891, and from 1891 imperial governors ruled the colony, from Julius von Soden to the last, Heinrich Schnee, from 1912 to 1918. Peters, named Reichskommissar for the Kilimanjaro Region in 1891 under Soden, was recalled in 1892 and in 1897, after three investigations, deprived of his commission, his title and his pension; Kaiser Wilhelm II nevertheless gave him the title of 'retired Reichskommissar' in 1905.

The administration relied heavily on African chiefs to keep order and collect taxes, and the labour ordinances issued in Dar es Salaam were largely ignored in the interior. The scandals of corruption and brutality that followed the Maji Maji war led Chancellor Bernhard von Bülow to appoint Bernhard Dernburg in 1907 to reform the colonial administration, and under Albrecht von Rechenberg, governor from 1906 to 1912, policy turned to African small-holder farming, for which railways were built. The government ran elementary, secondary and vocational schools for Africans. Its records from 1884 to 1917, held by the Tanzania National Archives, were inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 1997.
sections.impact:
German East Africa covered 994,996 square kilometres, nearly three times the area of present-day Germany, and took in present-day Burundi, Rwanda, mainland Tanzania and the Kionga Triangle. The agreements of 1886 and 1890 between Berlin and London drew the line that became the border of Kenya and Tanzania, surveyed from the sea to Mount Kilimanjaro in 1892 and on to Lake Victoria twelve years later. The Central Railroad, 1,247 kilometres long, linked Dar es Salaam with Morogoro, Tabora and Kigoma, and harbours were fitted with electric cranes, rail access and warehouses; in 1912 Dar es Salaam and Tanga received 356 steamers and over 1,000 coastal vessels. Rainer Tetzlaff nevertheless concluded that the colony never achieved any real significance for the German Empire, as a settlement, a supplier of raw materials or a market.

For its African peoples the colony meant conquest, forced labour and the famine of the Maji Maji war. Some of its institutions outlasted it: in 1924 the visiting Phelps-Stokes Commission judged that the German schools had met standards unmatched in tropical Africa, and the Swahili word for school, shule, comes from the German Schule. German spellings of local names, such as 'Kilimandscharo', stayed in use for a while. The Askari who fought in the East African campaign later received pensions from the Weimar Republic and West Germany.
sections.decline:
Germany's defeat in the First World War ended the colony. Outnumbered and short of supplies after forces from the Belgian Congo had attacked from the west, in the Battle of Tabora, Lettow-Vorbeck abandoned the colony, withdrew south into Portuguese Mozambique and then into Northern Rhodesia, and agreed to a ceasefire on hearing of the armistice concluded three days earlier. A smaller campaign on the southern shore of Lake Tanganyika in 1914 and 1915 had pitted a makeshift British and Belgian flotilla against the garrison at Bismarckburg. In Germany Lettow-Vorbeck was acclaimed as a hero and his Schutztruppe celebrated as the only German colonial force not defeated in open combat, though it often retreated when outnumbered.

On 7 May 1919 the Supreme Council of the Paris Peace Conference awarded all of German East Africa to Britain, over Belgium's strenuous objections. By the Anglo-Belgian agreement of 30 May 1919, negotiated by Alfred Milner and Pierre Orts, Britain ceded the north-western districts of Ruanda and Urundi to Belgium; on 12 July the Commission on Mandates gave the Kionga Triangle south of the Rovuma River to Portugal, reasoning that Germany had virtually forced Portugal to cede it in 1894. The Treaty of Versailles took effect on 10 January 1920, when the territory passed to the three powers and the British part took the name Tanganyika.

summary: German East Africa grew from Carl Peters' treaties and an imperial charter of 1885 into Germany's largest and most populous colony. Its conquest, forced labour and the famine that crushed the Maji Maji Rebellion cost hundreds of thousands of lives; after the First World War it was divided between Britain, Belgium and Portugal.
references: Byron Farwell, The Great War in Africa, 1914–1918 (W. W. Norton & Company, 1989)
A. L. C. Bullock, Germany's Colonial Demands (Oxford University Press, 1939)
Heinrich Schnee, German Colonization, Past and Future: The Truth about the German Colonies (George Allen & Unwin, 1926)
British Foreign Office, Treatment of Natives in the German Colonies (H. M. Stationery Office, 1920)

pointDescs.1885: Bismarck signs an imperial charter for Carl Peters' company, and five German warships force the Sultan of Zanzibar to accept German claims on the mainland beyond a 16-kilometre coastal strip.
pointDescs.1886: Germany and Britain agree to respect the Sultan's islands and coastal strip and divide the mainland into spheres of interest; German rule is established over Bagamoyo, Dar es Salaam and Kilwa.
pointDescs.1888: The Abushiri Revolt rises against the German East Africa Company; the German military is called in and puts it down with British help the following year.
pointDescs.1890: The Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty gives Heligoland to Germany and fixes the border with the British East Africa Protectorate.
pointDescs.1891: Imperial governors take over from the Reichskommissar, beginning with Julius von Soden; the Hehe under Chief Mkwawa begin their resistance, defeated by 1894.
pointDescs.1898: Mkwawa, cornered after years of guerrilla war, kills himself; gold has been found near Lake Victoria since 1894.
pointDescs.1905: The Maji Maji Rebellion breaks out and is crushed by Governor von Götzen through measures to create a famine, which may have cost as many as 300,000 lives.
pointDescs.1907: After scandals of corruption and brutality, Bernhard Dernburg is appointed to reform the colonial administration; Governor Rechenberg turns policy towards African small-holder farming and railways.
pointDescs.1912: Dar es Salaam and Tanga receive 356 steamers and over 1,000 coastal vessels; Heinrich Schnee becomes the last governor.
pointDescs.1914: The Central Railroad reaches Lake Tanganyika in July; in November Lettow-Vorbeck's forces defeat a British force more than eight times larger at the Battle of Tanga.
pointDescs.1915: The cruiser SMS Königsberg is scuttled in the Rufiji delta and her guns join the land forces; a campaign is fought on southern Lake Tanganyika.
pointDescs.1918: Pressed by greater numbers and short of supplies, Lettow-Vorbeck has left the colony for Mozambique and Northern Rhodesia, where he agrees to a ceasefire after the armistice; Schnee's governorship ends.
pointDescs.1919: The Paris Peace Conference awards the colony to Britain, which cedes Ruanda and Urundi to Belgium; the Kionga Triangle goes to Portugal.

notes: The register's end is 1919 (the Paris Peace Conference's awards); the formal transfer to Britain, Belgium and Portugal took effect on 10 January 1920, when the Treaty of Versailles came into force.

The capital is not named as such in the article; Dar es Salaam is given because the colony's ordinances were promulgated there and it held the garrison and the 'capital' celebration of July 1914. Earlier seats (Bagamoyo) are not stated and are left out.

The 'Battle of Tabora' is named without a date, and the year of Lettow-Vorbeck's ceasefire is not stated (only 'three days' after the armistice); the 1918 point rests on that and on Schnee's term ending in 1918.
The article's 'rival tribes' is written as 'rival peoples'. The Phelps-Stokes Commission's praise of German schools is quoted in substance, not word for word.

References come from the article's Further reading (its References section is empty in the saved text); places of publication are left off. East's unpublished thesis and Sievers' Afrika (in German) are not listed.
